articles.title: Scientists discover how harmful “zombie cells” hide from the immune system
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered a protein that may help harmful aging cells hide from the immune system, allowing them to accumulate and fuel age-related health problems. Blocking the protein in mice reduced these cells and inflammation while improving blood sugar regulation and strength, offering a promising new direction for anti-aging research.
articles.content:
Researchers led by Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University have discovered a protein that may allow harmful aging cells to escape detection by the immune system. By helping these cells remain in the body instead of being cleared away, the protein could contribute to their accumulation and the development of health problems associated with aging.

The discovery, published in Cell Metabolism, identifies PD-L2 as a potential target for therapies aimed at eliminating harmful aging cells. Scientists also believe the protein could serve as a blood marker, providing a way to detect and monitor these cells.

"Our findings suggest that PD-L2 may help aging cells stay in the body when they would normally be removed by the immune system," said Selim Chaib, PhD, research assistant professor of Medicine at Cedars-Sinai and first and co-corresponding author of the study.

How Harmful Aging Cells Escape the Immune System

As cells age or become damaged, some enter a state known as senescence. These cells stop dividing but remain alive, lingering in tissues rather than disappearing. Over time, they can accumulate and release substances that trigger inflammation and disrupt the normal activity of surrounding cells.

The buildup of these senescent cells has been associated with a range of health problems that become more common with age. Understanding why they persist, particularly when the immune system would normally remove them, could help scientists develop new ways to reduce their harmful effects.

The researchers found that PD-L2 may play an important role in this process by helping aging cells avoid immune clearance.

Blocking PD-L2 Reduces Aging Cells in Mice

To investigate the protein's role, scientists conducted experiments in laboratory mice in which PD-L2 was either removed or blocked. Both approaches reduced the accumulation of senescent cells and lowered levels of the inflammatory substances they release.

The benefits extended beyond changes at the cellular level. Mice with reduced PD-L2 activity also showed improvements in their ability to process sugar and demonstrated greater grip strength, suggesting that targeting the protein could influence physical functions affected by aging.

The team also examined human cells and tissues. They discovered that senescent human cells produced more PD-L2 than younger cells and that levels of the protein rose with age in certain human tissues. These findings suggest the mechanism observed in mice may also be relevant to human aging.

A Potential New Target for Age-Related Diseases

The results raise the possibility that blocking PD-L2 could help the immune system recognize and eliminate harmful aging cells, potentially reducing some of the health problems associated with their buildup.

"If we can find a way to block this protein, we may be able to help the immune system get rid of these cells and potentially improve health problems linked with aging," said James Kirkland, MD, PhD, director of the Center for Advanced Gerotherapeutics and senior author of the study.

Although the findings are promising, more research is needed before the approach can be considered for treating people. Future studies will investigate whether blocking PD-L2 is safe and can deliver meaningful health benefits in humans. Researchers also hope to clarify how the protein contributes to diseases associated with aging.

Additional Cedars-Sinai researchers who contributed to the study include Larissa Langhi Prata, Masayoshi Suda, Andres Sola, Jia Nie, Hyungsoo Kim, Tamar Pirtskhalava, Nino Giorgadze, Nicolas Musi, Ze'ev Ronai, and Tamara Tchkonia.

Other contributing authors were Thomas Mitchell, Zacharias Anastasiadis, Hawley Kunz, Stella Victorelli, Ricardo Lozano Flores, Moritz Weigl, Shimpei Kawamoto, Ken Uemura, Binsheng Wang, Christina Inman, Ailing Xue, Kurt Johnson, Jair Espindola-Netto, Sonja Suvakov, Jennet Hatamova, Erik Parker, Davyn Benitto Hartono, Vagisha Kulshreshtha, Jose Alberto Lopez-Dominguez, Aaron Deisinger, Allyson Palmer, Yi Zhu, Megan Weivoda, Anne Gingery, Robert Hromas, Vesna Garovic, João Passos, David Allison, Eiji Hara, Michael Jensen, Stefan Tullius, Manuel Serrano, Ming Xu, Ian Lanza, and Yuji Ikeno.

Ryan, the Hevolution Foundation, and the Noaber Foundation. Y.I. was supported by the San Antonio Nathan Shock Center Pathology Core (NIH Grant P30AG13319), San Antonio Claude D. 445 Pepper Center (NIH P30 AG044271), and NIH grants R01AG070034 and R56AG057785. M.D.J.'s studies were supported by NIH grants DK-45343 and DK-40484. H.E.K. was supported by an NIH musculoskeletal research training grant (T32AR56950) and NIH grant K01DK134765. S.K. was supported by the Japan Science and Technology Agency (JST) JPMJFR2308 and Japan Society for the Promotion of Science (JSPS) JP23K06481. L.G.P.L.P was supported by NIH grant 1K01AG090692. The clinical trial (NCT03350906) was supported by grants UL1TR002377 from the National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences (NCATS) and NIH R01AG054454. Y.Z. was supported by the Hevolution Foundation. J.F.P. was supported by NIH grants R01AG068048, R01AG82708, and UG3CA268103 and the Glenn Foundation for Medical Research. S.V.G. is supported by a Robert and Arlene Kogod Center on Aging Career Development Award and a c-SiG Pilot and Feasibility Award. A.G. was supported by NIH grant R01AR076347. M.X. is supported by a Hevolution/AFAR New Investigator Award in Biology and Geroscience Research. This work was supported in part by NIH P30AG050886.

M.S. is a shareholder of Senolytic Therapeutics, Life Biosciences, Rejuveron Senescence Therapeutics, and Altos Labs. articles.title: PM launches brain cancer review after meeting 'inspirational' patient
articles.summary: The Scottish athlete, who has inoperable brain tumours, previously made a tearful plea for more investment in brain cancer research on BBC Breakfast.
articles.content:
Swimmer Archie Goodburn has been successful in his efforts to improve brain cancer care for patients as the UK government announce new measures.

The Scottish athlete, who was diagnosed with three inoperable brain tumours two years ago, met Prime Minister Andy Burnham after making a tearful TV appeal for more investment to be put into brain cancer research.

After the meeting, Burnham announced a new national brain cancer clinical lead and promised a review of brain cancer progress and action to get patients treatment sooner.

Goodburn, 25, thanked the prime minister and said all three of his requests have been "promised to some extent" but "fleshing out" needs to be done on the details.

The prime minister described the swimmer an "inspiration to us all" and said he was "delighted" to welcome him to Downing Street.

Burnham said: "He has spoken passionately about the need for change on brain cancer, and he's right: progress hasn't been good enough, here or anywhere else.

"Families facing this disease can't afford to wait."

Goodburn reached the final of the 50m breaststroke at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

He said he went for medical tests after suffering from numbness and seizures during training for the 2024 Olympic trials.

He was diagnosed with three large oligodendrogliomas, a rare type of cancer which can affect the brain and spinal cord.

The Edinburgh-born athlete underwent chemotherapy and radiotherapy to treat the tumours, but surgery to remove them was found to be impossible.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant positive development in brain cancer care prompted by an inspirational patient's advocacy, leading to government action including appointing a national clinical lead and a review to improve treatment access. This has broad societal impact for patients with brain cancer and is well detailed.

articles.title: Scientists may have overlooked a hidden Alzheimer's culprit for decades
articles.summary: For decades, scientists have focused on amyloid beta as a major culprit behind Alzheimer’s disease, spending billions of dollars developing treatments that have often delivered disappointing results. Now, researchers at UC Santa Cruz are drawing attention to a largely overlooked peptide called P3 that could also play a role in the disease. Previously believed to be harmless, P3 can form harmful-looking protein clumps even faster than amyloid beta and may also damage brain cells.
articles.content:
For decades, researchers have invested billions of dollars in Alzheimer's treatments designed to target amyloid beta, a peptide that forms harmful deposits in the brain. But a biochemist at the University of California, Santa Cruz, believes scientists may have overlooked another potential contributor to the disease: a smaller, closely related peptide that was long considered harmless.

In a new commentary published in ChemBioChem, UC Santa Cruz professor Jevgenij Raskatov highlights research suggesting that this lesser-known peptide, called P3, can form microscopic clumps and threadlike structures known as fibrils. Evidence also suggests that P3 may interact with amyloid beta (Aβ), potentially influencing how it accumulates in the brain and how toxic it becomes. These findings raise the possibility that P3 contributes to the nerve cell damage associated with Alzheimer's disease.

"The P3 peptide is, most likely, not the innocent bystander it was commonly thought to be. There's still more research to be done. But this could turn Alzheimer's research on its head," said Raskatov, whose laboratory investigates amyloid peptides in hopes of identifying ways to prevent their harmful effects and develop better Alzheimer's treatments. "P3 is a distinct aggregating peptide that is itself potentially neurotoxic and may be contributing to Alzheimer's disease."

Why Alzheimer's Treatments Have Had Limited Success

Alzheimer's is the most widespread neurodegenerative disease, affecting approximately 35 million people worldwide and generating annual costs exceeding $800 billion. The number of people living with the condition is expected to double by 2050.

Despite decades of intensive research, developing effective treatments has proved extraordinarily difficult. More than 400 clinical trials have investigated potential Alzheimer's drugs, with most focusing on amyloid beta. Many of these efforts have failed, while others have produced only modest benefits. Some treatments have also been associated with serious complications, including brain hemorrhages and strokes.

Amyloid beta originates from a much larger protein embedded in cell membranes called the Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP). Two enzymes, β-secretase and γ-secretase, cut this protein in sequence, releasing amyloid beta peptides of different lengths.

Researchers have concentrated particularly on two versions, Aβ40 and Aβ42, which contain 40 and 42 amino acids, respectively. Aβ42 has attracted the greatest attention because it is especially prone to sticking together and forming toxic aggregates. As a result, it has remained a central target of Alzheimer's drug development for decades.

Existing medications, including cholinesterase inhibitors and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonists, can temporarily ease certain symptoms but do not stop the disease from progressing. More recently, antibody treatments such as Lecanemab and Donanemab have been approved to help remove amyloid beta from the brain.

However, Raskatov argues that the benefits achieved so far remain limited, underscoring the need to investigate other biological processes involved in Alzheimer's.

"Progress has been extremely slow, and the current state of the art in Alzheimer's therapy leaves much to be desired," he said. "We need fundamentally new approaches to the problem."

The Overlooked Peptide That May Also Damage Brain Cells

Unlike amyloid beta, P3 forms when Amyloid Precursor Protein is processed through a different sequence of molecular cuts. In this pathway, an enzyme called α-secretase acts first, followed by γ-secretase.

Raskatov has proposed calling this peptide "Amyloid α," or Aα, to better distinguish it from amyloid beta and reflect its ability to form aggregates.

For years, scientists largely assumed that P3 was incapable of forming amyloid deposits, was not toxic to cells, and would remain soluble in water. Under that interpretation, the peptide would simply dissolve rather than accumulate in the brain.

These assumptions were never adequately verified, according to Raskatov. Nevertheless, they helped establish the view that P3 was unlikely to matter in Alzheimer's disease, leaving it largely absent from research efforts.

Raskatov, a specialist in peptide chemistry, and researchers in his laboratory decided to test those long-standing beliefs.

Over the past five years, the team has published three major studies demonstrating that P3 can form amyloid deposits at least as readily as amyloid beta. In fact, their experiments showed that P3 produces these aggregates more rapidly.

The researchers also found evidence that P3 itself may be harmful to neurons, although its toxicity appears lower than that of amyloid beta.

According to Raskatov, an independent research group in the United Kingdom has confirmed and expanded upon his team's findings. Other laboratories are now beginning to investigate how P3 and amyloid beta interact, including whether their relationship affects the accumulation and toxicity of these peptides.

Together, the results challenge the long-held assumption that P3 is biologically harmless and irrelevant to Alzheimer's. However, further research is needed to establish whether and how it contributes to the disease in patients.

Challenging Decades of Alzheimer's Research

For much of the past several decades, amyloid beta has dominated scientific explanations of Alzheimer's disease. David Teplow, an emeritus professor of neurology at UCLA and a prominent Alzheimer's researcher, said the peptide has long been regarded as a central cause of the condition.

But an independent evaluation of Raskatov's research led Teplow to conclude that scientists are beginning to reconsider this narrow focus.

"This reevaluation has far-reaching consequences for both basic science and clinical research into the causes and treatment of Alzheimer's disease," said Teplow, a founding editorial board member of the Journal of Molecular Neuroscience and the American Journal of Neurodegenerative Disease, as well as editor-in-chief of Progress in Molecular Biology and Translational Science.

Raskatov has also encountered a troubling problem while examining how other scientists have interpreted his team's discoveries.

He identified at least four papers published in respected, peer-reviewed journals that cited his laboratory's research as evidence that P3 was harmless and unable to form amyloid deposits. Yet his team's experiments had demonstrated precisely the opposite.

"This is exactly the opposite of what we have actually shown," Raskatov said. "We remain in the dark on how this sort of grand confusion may have come about. Clearly, there is more work ahead of us."

The emerging evidence suggests that understanding Alzheimer's may require looking beyond amyloid beta alone. By examining P3 and its interactions with other amyloid peptides, researchers hope to gain a more complete picture of the processes that damage brain cells and potentially identify new directions for treatment.

This new insight challenges decades of focus on amyloid beta alone and opens promising avenues for better understanding and potentially more effective treatments for a widespread and devastating condition affecting millions globally. The story has broad significance for public health and contains detailed context about the discovery and its implications.

Cela pourrait ouvrir de nouvelles pistes pour le développement de médicaments et améliorer les chances de trouver des traitements efficaces.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Des scientifiques ont découvert que le peptide négligé P3 pourrait contribuer à la maladie d’Alzheimer, offrant une nouvelle direction pour la recherche et le développement de traitements.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos encuentran un nuevo péptido que podría estar involucrado en el Alzheimer
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante muchos años, los científicos que estudian el Alzheimer se han centrado principalmente en una proteína llamada beta-amiloide. Esta proteína puede formar grupos en el cerebro que están relacionados con la enfermedad. A pesar de gastar miles de millones en tratamientos dirigidos a la beta-amiloide, los avances han sido lentos y a menudo decepcionantes.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores de la Universidad de California en Santa Cruz, encabezados por el profesor Jevgenij Raskatov, descubrieron que otro péptido llamado P3, que antes se creía inofensivo, también puede formar grupos dañinos en el cerebro. Sus estudios muestran que P3 forma estos grupos incluso más rápido que la beta-amiloide y puede dañar las células cerebrales. Esto desafía la creencia de que P3 no estaba involucrado en el Alzheimer.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo es importante porque sugiere que los científicos podrían haber pasado por alto una pieza clave del rompecabezas del Alzheimer. Si el P3 contribuye al daño cerebral, enfocarse solo en la beta-amiloide podría explicar por qué muchos tratamientos han tenido éxito limitado. Entender cómo P3 y la beta-amiloide trabajan juntos podría conducir a nuevas y mejores formas de tratar o prevenir el Alzheimer.

**Próximo paso** – Se necesita más investigación para confirmar cómo afecta el P3 al cerebro y su papel en el Alzheimer. Otros laboratorios están comenzando a estudiar el P3, su interacción con la beta-amiloide y cómo estos péptidos causan daño. Esto podría abrir nuevos caminos para el desarrollo de medicamentos y mejorar las posibilidades de encontrar tratamientos efectivos.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Científicos han descubierto que el péptido P3, antes ignorado, podría contribuir al Alzheimer, ofreciendo una nueva dirección para la investigación y el desarrollo de tratamientos.

articles.title: Health workers tackle taboos over drinking with new AI tool
articles.summary: A new AI-powered hub for health professionals aims to help identify alcohol-related risks and launch discussions with patients, including the link between drinking and cancer, the World Health Organization (WHO) announced on Wednesday.
articles.content:
“Alcohol harm isn’t abstract,” said Dr. Carina Ferreira-Borges, the WHO Europe regional adviser on alcohol. “It can be heart and liver disease. It can be a baby exposed to alcohol before birth. It can be anxiety and depression. It can be a woman who develops breast cancer without ever being told alcohol was a risk.”

The launch highlighted the widespread lack of awareness about alcohol-related health risks.

‘Not an awkward extra’

“We know screening and brief interventions work, but only if health professionals feel able to use them” she continued.

“A doctor or nurse with a few minutes between patients can now ask the hub’s AI assistant how to ask about alcohol consumption and get an answer based on WHO evidence. That makes conversations about alcohol a normal part of care, not an awkward extra.”

Only 15 per cent of people surveyed in 14 European Union countries know that alcohol can cause breast cancer, WHO said, adding that it actually causes at least seven types of cancer as well as cardiovascular and liver disease.

“Alcohol is so deeply embedded in our cultures and social lives that even doctors and nurses can feel uncomfortable asking patients about it, particularly when the patient has come in for something seemingly unrelated,” said Dr. Ferreira-Borges. “Add time pressures, limited training and uncertainty about how to approach the subject without sounding judgemental and you have a major missed opportunity for prevention.”

Tweet URL

Prevention opportunities

To address this gap, WHO Europe has launched its new alcohol screening and brief interventions hub, which brings together evidence, guidance and practical tools to help health professionals discuss alcohol-related risks.

Health workers can begin with a 10-question screening test to assess a patient’s alcohol-related risk then use the hub’s AI assistant to prepare for a conversation or find relevant guidance.

“The science is evolving and keeping up with the evidence on alcohol and its links to more than 200 diseases and health conditions is not always straightforward,” Dr. Ferreira-Borges noted.

Catching links

Alcohol is among the least frequently discussed behavioural risk factors in healthcare, WHO noted, and is raised less often than smoking, physical activity or diet.

Many health professionals have been trained to recognise the symptoms associated with heavy drinking, “but not necessarily to understand and communicate the risks associated with more routine consumption”, Dr. Ferreira-Borges continued.

“Say they have a patient with high blood pressure or mental health issues, alcohol rarely comes up, even though it can play an important role.”

articles.personality_title: New AI tool helps health workers talk about alcohol risks

**What happened** – The World Health Organization (WHO) has created a new online tool powered by artificial intelligence (AI) to help health workers. Launched recently, this tool guides doctors and nurses on how to ask patients about their drinking habits and explain the risks, such as the link between alcohol and cancer. It also offers a quick test to check a patient's alcohol-related risks.

**Impact** – This tool is important because many people don’t realize how harmful alcohol can be. For example, only 15% of people in some European countries know that alcohol can cause breast cancer. The tool makes it easier for health workers to include alcohol discussions in normal care, even when patients come for other reasons. This could help catch problems earlier and encourage healthier choices.

**What's next step** – Health professionals across Europe and possibly worldwide will start using this AI tool to improve conversations about alcohol. The WHO will continue updating the tool with the latest research to keep it useful and easy to use. Over time, this could lead to fewer alcohol-related illnesses.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new AI tool from WHO helps doctors and nurses talk openly with patients about the health risks of drinking alcohol, making prevention easier and more effective.

articles.personality_title_es: Nueva herramienta de IA ayuda a profesionales de salud a hablar sobre riesgos del alcohol
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Beber alcohol puede causar muchos problemas de salud, como enfermedades del corazón, del hígado, cáncer y problemas mentales. Pero muchas personas, incluidos médicos y enfermeros, encuentran difícil hablar sobre el consumo de alcohol durante las consultas. Esto dificulta la prevención.

**Qué pasó** – La Organización Mundial de la Salud (OMS) creó una nueva herramienta en línea con inteligencia artificial (IA) para ayudar a los profesionales de salud. Lanzada recientemente, esta herramienta guía a médicos y enfermeros para preguntar a los pacientes sobre su consumo de alcohol y explicar los riesgos, como la relación entre alcohol y cáncer. También ofrece una prueba rápida para evaluar riesgos.

**Impacto** – Esta herramienta es importante porque muchas personas no saben cuán dañino puede ser el alcohol. Por ejemplo, solo el 15 % de la gente en algunos países europeos sabe que el alcohol puede causar cáncer de mama. La herramienta facilita que los profesionales de salud hablen sobre alcohol en la atención normal, incluso cuando el paciente viene por otro motivo. Esto puede ayudar a detectar problemas antes y promover hábitos más saludables.

**Próximo paso** – Los profesionales de salud en Europa y posiblemente en todo el mundo comenzarán a usar esta herramienta de IA para mejorar las conversaciones sobre el alcohol. La OMS seguirá actualizando la herramienta con la investigación más reciente para mantenerla útil y fácil de usar. Con el tiempo, esto podría reducir las enfermedades relacionadas con el alcohol.

**Una frase clave** – Una nueva herramienta de IA de la OMS ayuda a médicos y enfermeros a hablar abiertamente con los pacientes sobre los riesgos del alcohol, facilitando la prevención.
